rules.name: Order of the unit rules, and the unwrap fix
rules.trigger: Insert the rules in this order. (1) Coordinates, before Temperatures and before the new Heights rule (5'11"). (2) Slash compounds, before the existing m/s² and ²/³ area rules and before `units`. (3) Square and cubic word forms, next to the existing ²/³ area rule. (4) Hyphenated number-unit modifiers. (5) Fraction + unit, before the mixed-fraction, 'Fractions' and '½ cup' rules. (6) `units` and gluedUnits with the extended table, plus the per-symbol guards (nm, MW, ppm, hp, atm, kn, mo, MJ). (7) Conditional units: carat (before the money K rule), pt, cal, in., psi. (8) Single-letter units, with A last.
rules.risks: Since the fix3/reading merge, Heights runs right after Temperatures. So '40°42'46"N' reads 'forty degrees forty-two foot forty-six N' today, and coordinates must take the whole span first. Every context check (A's electrical words, W's allowlist, label words, size tokens, network words, sea words) must read the whole sentence with lexicon marks reduced to their text, as readArrow and readRomanNumerals do. The rules see only the plain chunk between marks, and USB-C, LED, EV, PSU, RMS, Qi, MagSafe, ATM and HP are tech-lexicon marks. For example, '65 W USB-C charger' reaches the rules as '65 W '. A bug to fix as well: normalize(skippingMarkedSpans:) turns a unit term back into plain text whenever a number precedes it, even when no rule then reads it. The `units` rule refuses a unit followed by '/', so today '300 kWh/yr' reads 'three hundred kwer', '5 mm/s' reads 'five m S' and '20 ms/frame' comes out garbled. Unwrap only when a rule will consume the term.

rules.name: Coordinates: degrees with a compass letter
rules.trigger: A number, then °, then optional minutes with a prime, then optional seconds with a double prime, then one capital N, S, E or W that is not followed by a letter or digit. Sketch: (?<![\p{L}\d.])(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d+)?)\s?°\s?(?:(\d{1,2}(?:\.\d+)?)\s?[′'’]\s?(?:(\d{1,2}(?:\.\d+)?)\s?(?:″|"|”|′′|'')\s?)?)?([NSEW])(?![\p{L}\d]). Spaces are allowed between the parts ('51.5° N').
rules.reads_as: '<d> degree(s)[ <m> minute(s)][ <s> second(s)] north|south|east|west'. Each unit is singular only when its value is exactly 1. Numbers stay as digits. Examples: '45°30′N' → '45 degrees 30 minutes north'; '0.1° W' → '0.1 degrees west'; '34° S' → '34 degrees south'.
rules.risks: It requires °, so heights (5'10") and a bare '45 N' are untouched. °C and °F never match, because C and F aren't compass letters ('45°C' is a regression case). Today Temperatures strands the letter: '45°N' reads 'forty-five N', and '0.1° W' reads 'degrees double-u'. The rule must also run before W as watts. The numbers area drops a trailing zero ('74.0060'), so the tests avoid trailing zeros.

rules.name: Slash compounds read as 'per'
rules.where: TextNormalizer.rules: new rule before the area rules and `units`
rules.trigger: A number (lookbehind (?<![\p{L}\d.,/])), an optional space, a NUMERATOR, then one or more '/DENOMINATOR', then (?![\p{L}\d/]). The unit may be spaced or glued ('7GB/s', '5mm/s'). NUMERATOR is any symbol in `units` or gluedUnits, plus g, m, L, l, W, V, mmol, mol and µmol. Lexicon terms the unwrap returns (kWh, mm, ms, GB) count. DENOMINATOR maps to a singular word: s/sec → second; s² → second squared; min → minute; h/hr → hour; d/day → day; wk → week; mo → month; yr → year; g → gram; kg → kilogram; mg → milligram; L/l → liter; mL/ml → milliliter; dL/dl → deciliter; m → meter; km → kilometer; cm → centimeter; mi → mile; ft → foot; gal → gallon; m² → square meter; m³ → cubic meter; cm³ → cubic centimeter; kWh → kilowatt hour; serving. Fixed specials: 'L/100km', 'L/100 km' and 'l/100km' → 'liters per hundred kilometers'; 'km/L' and 'km/l' → 'kilometers per liter'. km/h, m/s, mph and kph keep their existing rules, and the money rule keeps '$5/mo'.
rules.reads_as: '<numerator: singular for 1, else plural> per <denominator>[ per <denominator>]'. Examples: '5 mg/kg' → '5 milligrams per kilogram'; '5.5 mmol/L' → '5.5 millimoles per liter'; '300 kWh/yr' → '300 kilowatt hours per year'; '5 mm/s' → '5 millimeters per second'; '7GB/s' → '7 gigabytes per second'; '7.8 g/cm³' → '7.8 grams per cubic centimeter'; 'mg/kg/day' → '... per kilogram per day'.
rules.risks: It fires only after a number, and only when both sides are in the table. So 'and/or', 'w/', '24/7', '1/2', 'm/f' (f is not a denominator, frozen) and money are untouched. '/day' and '/yr' read 'per', matching money's '/month' (open question 9). Today '5.5 mmol/L' drops '/L', 'mg/kg' reads as letters, '300 kWh/yr' reads 'kwer', '5 mm/s' reads 'm S' and '7GB/s' reads 'G B S'. Spaced '7 GB/s' already works through a tech-lexicon key.

rules.name: Square and cubic word forms (the ²/³ symbols already work)
rules.where: TextNormalizer: extend the existing area rule ('50 km²') with a word-form table
rules.trigger: Already shipped: '²'/'³' after km, cm, mm, μm, m, ft, in, yd or mi, and m/s². Still to add, after a number with an optional space: 'sq ft', 'sq. ft.', 'sq.ft.', 'sqft', 'Sq Ft', 'Sq. Ft.', 'SQ FT', 'sq m', 'sqm', 'sq km', 'sq mi', 'sq in', 'sq yd'; 'cu ft', 'cu. ft.', 'cu in', 'cu yd', 'cu m'; the '^2'/'^3' forms; ft² and in² written with a dot. Also lower-case 'm2'/'m3', but only when followed by the end of the text, punctuation, or one of flat, apartment, house, home, office, room, plot, space, garden, of, per; and never when the sentence has slot(s), SSD, NVMe, drive(s), chip, Mac or MacBook. In the dotted forms, swallow the final '.' only before a lower-case word or a comma.
rules.reads_as: 'square <unit>' or 'cubic <unit>': singular for 1 ('1 sq ft' → '1 square foot'), plural otherwise ('800 square feet', '85 square meters', '20 cubic feet').
rules.risks: Today 'sq ft' reads 'S Q ft' and 'cu ft' reads 'cue ft'. 'cc' after a number deliberately stays the letters C C (frozen). Capital M2/M3 (the motorway, the chip, M.2 slots) is never matched. Lower-case 'm2 slots' is guarded (frozen).

rules.name: More multi-letter symbols in the `units` table
rules.where: TextNormalizer.units (case-sensitive, after a number, spaced or glued), plus unitTerms
rules.reads_as: '<number> <singular if 1 or -1, else plural>', as the existing table does. Examples: '1 atm' → '1 atmosphere'; '4,000 mAh' → '4,000 milliamp hours'; '300 hp' → '300 horsepower'; '6 mo' → '6 months'.
rules.risks: The tech lexicon marks dB, HPA and MPA (case-insensitive, so it catches hPa and MPa), PKG (case-insensitive), GW (plural), MWh/GWh/TWh, nm, ns, PB and KT. Putting them in `units` puts them in unitTerms, so after a number they read through this table, and elsewhere the lexicon stands ('the dB scale'). unitTerms also needs 'pkgs', or should strip a plural suffix. Only lower-case hp (HP is the brand), atm (ATM), qt (Qt, said 'cute') and mo. Leave bar, BTU, rpm, bhp and cc alone (frozen). An existing false positive: '5 min' as minimum ('Order 5 min, 10 max') already reads 'five minutes'.

rules.name: nm: nautical miles near sea or air words
rules.trigger: A number, an optional space, then nm, when the sentence has a sea or air word: offshore, ship, boat, vessel, yacht, ferry, sail(s/ed/ing), harbour, harbor, coast, coastline, nautical, knot(s), kts, aircraft, flight, flew, fly, plane, airport, runway, pilot.
rules.reads_as: '<number> nautical mile(s)': '12 nm offshore' → '12 nautical miles offshore'. Anywhere else it is nanometer(s), singular for 1 ('a 3 nm process', '1 nm thick').
rules.risks: Pilots and sailors write nm for nautical miles, and today 'twelve nanometers offshore' is absurd. Without those words the tech reading stands. A chip sentence has none of them.

rules.name: Single-letter units: m, g, L/l, V, W, h, s
rules.where: TextNormalizer: new rule after the slash, area and `units` rules, before Ranges
rules.trigger:
A number (lookbehind (?<![\p{L}\d.,/]); a leading minus or a range dash is fine, but not '<letter>-' as in 'W-2L'), an optional space, the letter, then (?![\p{L}\d'’&*+\-/²³°]), and not '.' + a letter.
Shared guards. Skip when:
- a currency symbol precedes the number;
- the word before the number is a label word (the author's list plus sector, wing, level, pier, dock, hall, concourse, aisle, locker, slot) or any capitalised word that doesn't start the sentence;
- the letter is W, L, H or D in a dimension group with x/× on either side;
- the same sentence has a glued W-number and L-number pair ('32W 34L', '3W 2L').
Per letter:
- m (lower case). Spaced → meter(s), unless the next word is ago, left, late, later, early, remaining, or a count noun (people, users, viewers, customers, subscribers, followers, members, residents, voters, votes, visitors, downloads, views, streams, copies, units, jobs, homes, households, years, barrels, dollars, pounds, euros), or the sentence has money words (raised, revenue, funding, budget, sales, profit, valuation, worth, deal, invest*, debt, population). Glued → meters only before tall, high, long, deep, wide, thick, apart, across, below, above, underwater, or 'x <number>'. Removed 'away', 'ahead' and 'behind': 'I'm 5m away' means minutes in chat.
- g (lower case): gram(s), spaced or glued. Skip a glued 2–6 when the sentence has phone, signal, network, coverage, mobile, data, LTE, SIM, carrier, reception, wifi, internet, connection, rollout, mast, tower, broadband, router or hotspot. Skip g when the sentence has g-force words (pull*, force(s), pilot, jet, fighter, aircraft, coaster, rollercoaster, crash, impact, acceleration, centrifuge, astronaut).
- L and l: liter(s). Skip when the sentence has a clothing-size token (XS, S, M, XL, XXL) or size/sizes. Skip a glued L after 30–60 before suit, jacket, blazer or coat (L is Long). Skip a glued 1L–4L after a/as a/my/her/his/every, unless a container or liquid word follows (bottle, jug, carton, tank, flask, pot, pan, of, soda, water, juice, milk): 1L, 2L and 3L are law students.
- V: volt(s). Skip before a digit ('V8').
- W: watt(s). Skip before ' <digit or ordinal>', and before ' <Capitalised word>' unless that word is LED, LEDs, USB, USB-C, AC, DC, RMS, PSU, GaN, PD, Qi, MagSafe, CFL or PoE. A following hyphen ('5W-30') or digit ('10W40') is already excluded.
- h (lower case): hour(s). Skip after at, until, till, from, by, before or after when the number is 24 or less (European clock time, '18h'), and before digits ('10h30').
- s (lower case): second(s), only spaced ('30 s') or glued after a decimal ('1.5s'), never a glued integer.
rules.reads_as: '<number> <singular for 1 or -1, else plural>'. Examples: '25 m' → '25 meters'; '30m high' → '30 meters high'; '50g' → '50 grams'; '2L' → '2 liters'; '5V' → '5 volts'; '2,000 W' → '2,000 watts'; '24h' → '24 hours'; '1.5s' → '1.5 seconds'.
rules.risks: Every guard has a frozen near-miss: 3 m viewers, 2m downloads, 5m away, 9 g in a turn, 5g rollout, 4g on a phone, 42L suit, 32W 34L jeans, 3W 2L record, 1L/2L law students, L-plates, 5W-30, 10W40, Sector 7 W, until 18h, 2H pencil, plus the author's set (Room 12 L, Apartment 5 W, size 9 W, Route 9 W, 500 W Madison St., W-2, 5 W's, V8, V-neck, L-shaped, 2 L and 3 XL, 9 g's, 1990s, her 20s, Sizes 8 M). Capital M is never meters. Glued m before a noun ('the 100m final') stays 'M'.

rules.name: A as amps only with electrical context
rules.where: Same single-letter rule, with an extra condition for A
rules.trigger: A capital A after a number. The shared guards apply. The A is not followed by '-', an apostrophe, '*', '+', '.' + a letter, ' grade(s)', ' level(s)', ' star(s)' or ' Day'. Read it as amps only when the same sentence has another electrical unit after a number (V, W, mA, mAh, Ah, kW, Wh, Ω, Hz) or one of these words: volt(s), voltage, watt(s), amp(s), ampere(s), amperage, fuse(s), breaker(s), circuit(s), charger(s), charging, socket(s), outlet(s), adapter, adaptor, inverter, PSU, USB, wiring, electric, electrical. Removed from the author's list: current, rated, rating, draw(s), drew, load, motor, EV, battery, batteries, plug(s), cable(s), wire(s). Each has a common sense outside electricity ('current tally', 'rated 12A', 'a battery of exams').
rules.reads_as: '<number> amp(s)'. Examples: '5 V at 3 A' → '5 volts at 3 amps'; 'The fuse is rated at 13 A' → '13 amps'; 'Fit a 13 A fuse' → 'a 13 amp fuse'.
rules.risks: Frozen guards: 'rated 12A' (UK film certificate), 'current tally is 5 A', 'battery of exams … 4 A grades', '5 A* grades', 'Get your 5 A Day', 'Grade 5 A', '3 A-levels', 'Seat 12A', '4 AA batteries'. Today a lone A after a number reads as the article 'uh'. That belongs to the letters area, not this rule.

rules.name: Hyphenated number-unit modifiers
rules.where: TextNormalizer: new rule before Ranges and the unit rules. In normalize(skippingMarkedSpans:), widen the unwrap test from \d\s?$ to \d[\s-]?$.
rules.trigger: (?<![\p{L}\d.,/-])(\d+(?:[.,]\d+)?)-(UNIT)(?=\s+\p{Ll}), where UNIT is any table symbol, including km, kg, lb, ft, mi, yd, m, g, L, V, W, lower-case h, hr, min, mo and yr. Plus 'N-yr-old(s)' and 'N-mo-old(s)' → 'N year old(s)' and 'N month old(s)'.
rules.reads_as: '<number> <singular unit>', with the hyphen dropped. Examples: 'a 10-km run' → 'a 10 kilometer run'; 'a 5-lb bag' → 'a 5 pound bag'; 'a 12-hr shift' → 'a 12 hour shift'; 'Our 3-yr-old' → 'Our 3 year old'.
rules.risks: This fixes a real bug: today 'a 10-km run' and 'a 5-lb bag' lose their number. The rule needs a lower-case word after the unit. Compounds with the letter first are untouched (W-2, A-levels, T-shirts, L-shaped, V-neck, COVID-19), and so are '3-in-1' ('in' has no period) and '10-K'. Avoid heteronyms in tests ('a 2-min read').

rules.name: Fractions before a unit
rules.where: TextNormalizer: new rule before the mixed-fraction, 'Fractions' and '½ cup' rules
rules.trigger: Already handled today: slash fractions before a unit. '1/2 lb' reads 'one half pound' and '1 1/2 tsp' reads 'one and a half teaspoons'. Still to add: vulgar fractions before a table unit, either with no whole number ('½ tsp') or after one ('1½ tsp'). Today the `units` rule needs a digit right before the unit, so these spell the unit ('one and a half T S P'), and '1½ lb' reads 'one and a half pound'.
rules.reads_as: '½ tsp' → 'half a teaspoon' (open question 5); '1½ tsp' → '1 and a half teaspoons' (plural). Make the slash and vulgar forms read the same: today '1/2 lb' says 'one half pound'.
rules.risks: Only before a unit symbol, so '½ cup' and '1/2 the time' keep their fraction readings. ¼ is said 'a quarter teaspoon' in the US and 'a quarter of a teaspoon' in the UK, so it has no test.

rules.name: Singular unit after 'a'/'an' (open question 1)
rules.where: Inside each unit rule's replacement, looking back from the number
rules.trigger: The number directly follows 'a' or 'an' (any case), and the unit is followed by a lower-case word other than of, per, each, or, and, to, in, a, an, the, for.
rules.reads_as: The singular unit name: 'a 60 W bulb' → 'a 60 watt bulb'; 'a 13 A fuse' → 'a 13 amp fuse'; 'a 4 min mile' → 'a 4 minute mile'; 'a 3 nm process' → 'a 3 nanometer process'; 'a 2L bottle' → 'a 2 liter bottle'; 'a 1 ct diamond' → 'a 1 carat diamond'.
rules.risks: Narrow by design: it does not fire after 'the', so 'the 65 W charger' still reads the plural (a known miss). Today 'a 4 min mile' reads 'four minutes mile'. Seven tests depend on this decision.

rules.name: pt: pint or point, depending on the next word
rules.trigger: A number, an optional space, then pt or pt. Read 'pint(s)' before ' of', or before milk, cream, water, beer, ale, lager, stout, cider, stock, broth or juice. Read 'point' (always singular) before type, typeface, font, text, size, lettering, leading, line(s), margin, stroke, border, gutter, serif, sans, bold, italic or regular; before a capitalised font name; or when 'font' or 'type' appears earlier in the sentence. Optional and safe: lead, deficit, scale, shot, turn and plan also read 'point' ('a 3 pt shot').
rules.reads_as: '1 pt of cream' → '1 pint of cream'; '12 pt type' → '12 point type'.
rules.risks: Anything else stays the letters P T. In clinical notes pt means patient ('Saw 12 pt in clinic', frozen). 'pts' is not handled.

rules.name: Carat and knots: kt, ct, K
rules.where: TextNormalizer: before the single-letter rule and before the money K rule
rules.trigger: Carat. A number not preceded by a currency symbol, an optional space, then kt, Kt, KT, ct, K or k. Then optionally white, yellow, rose, solid or pure. Then gold, platinum, diamond(s), ruby, rubies, sapphire(s), emerald(s), gem(s), gemstone(s), stone(s), solitaire, ring(s), band, chain, necklace, bracelet, earrings or pendant. For kt/K/k (gold) the number must be 9, 10, 12, 14, 18, 22 or 24; for ct (gems) any number, decimals included. Knots: kts always (table), and kt alone when the sentence has wind(s), gust(s), gusting, breeze, headwind, tailwind, crosswind, airspeed, groundspeed, sea(s), boat, ship, vessel or aircraft, and none of bomb, nuclear, warhead, yield, blast, explosion or TNT.
rules.reads_as: '<number> carat', which never changes ('18kt gold ring' → '18 carat gold ring'; carat and karat sound the same). '1 ct diamond' → '1 carat diamond'. '15 kt winds' → '15 knot winds'.
rules.risks: Frozen guards: '$15K gold watch' (currency), 'yield of 21 kt' dropped from an aircraft (kilotons). Today '18kt' loses its number and '1 ct' reads 'one court'. Without these following words, kt (kiloton), ct (count) and K (thousand, kelvin) are left alone.

rules.name: cal: calories only before 'per'
rules.trigger: A number that doesn't start with '.', an optional space, then cal, followed by ' per', '/serving', '/day' or ' a day', and not followed by rifle, pistol, gun, round(s), ammo, bullet(s) or machine.
rules.reads_as: '100 cal per serving' → '100 calories per serving'. kcal goes through the main table.
rules.risks: cal is also calibre ('He fired the 50 cal.', frozen), so every other use stays 'cal'.

rules.name: Unit abbreviations with a period: in. (ft., tbsp. already work)
rules.where: TextNormalizer: an 'in.' entry, and an optional trailing '.' on the other table units
rules.trigger: 'in.' after a number means inches only when it is followed by a lower-case word, ' x '/'×', a digit, or one of , ; ). Today '3 ft. long' and '2 tbsp. of oil' already read correctly (both are regression cases). Extend the same handling to yd., lb., lbs., oz., gal., qt. and tsp., and to the hyphen and slash rules.
rules.risks: 'in' without a period is never a unit ('5 in a row', 'Put 2 in the oven', '3-in-1'). Before a capital, or at the end of the text, the period stays the full stop and 'in' stays the word ('Put 2 in. Then stir.', 'I put 5 in.', both frozen).

rules.name: psi read as letters (open question 2)
rules.trigger: A number, an optional space, then psi or PSI, followed by a non-letter.
rules.reads_as: The letters P S I: '35 psi' → '35 P S I' (or a phoneme mark).
rules.risks: Today psi and PSI read as the Greek letter ('sigh').

rules.name: Left alone on purpose
rules.trigger: Not handled: t/T (tonne, or teaspoon/tablespoon in US recipes); Mt (Mount, or megatonne); N (newton, or north); K alone (thousand, or kelvin); J alone; mb (millibar, or megabyte); ct without a gem word (carat, or count); pts; d (days, which belong to the timestamps area); glued m before a noun; capital M, HP and M2/M3; bar, BTU, rpm, bhp and cc; ppm near printer words; kn without boat words; 'the' + number + unit (attributive plural stays).
rules.risks: These are deliberate misses, which are safer than false positives. Field packs can add the insider readings.

open_questions: 1. Should 'a 60 W bulb' be read 'a sixty watt bulb', which is how people say it? Recommended: yes, but only right after 'a'/'an' and in hyphenated forms ('a 10-km run'), never after 'the'. Seven speech cases depend on this answer (60 W bulb, 13 A fuse, 4 min mile, 3 nm process, 2L bottle, 1 ct diamond, and indirectly 'a 5-min walk').
2. Should psi be read as letters ('thirty-five P S I', what drivers say) or as 'pounds per square inch'? Recommended: letters. Today it reads 'sigh'.

3. Should kcal be read 'kilocalories', 'calories' (how most people talk about food) or 'kay-cal'? Today's build already says 'kay-cal', which people do say. Recommended: 'kilocalories', which is correct for a general listener and never wrong.

4. Should mpg, ppm and mmHg be expanded ('miles per gallon', 'parts per million', 'millimeters of mercury') or read as letters? Recommended: expand them, except ppm near printer words (pages per minute), which stays letters. Units people only ever say as letters (rpm, BTU, bhp, cc) stay letters.

5. Should '½ tsp' be read 'half a teaspoon' or 'one half teaspoon'? Recommended: 'half a teaspoon'. Whichever wins, make '1/2 lb' agree with it: today it reads 'one half pound'. ¼ has no test, because the US says 'a quarter teaspoon' and the UK 'a quarter of a teaspoon'.

6. Glued 'm' can mean meters, million or minutes. Core reads it as meters only before a size word ('30m high', '2m apart'). Is it OK that 'the 100m final', '2m downloads' and 'I'm 5m away' keep reading 'M'? Recommended: yes.
7. Core leaves these as letters: t/T, pts, ct without a gem word, K, N, mb. Is that OK? Recommended: yes.
8. New: should nm be read 'nautical miles' when the sentence has sea or air words ('12 nm offshore'), instead of today's 'nanometers offshore'? Recommended: yes.
9. New: should '/yr' and '/day' after a unit be read 'per year', which matches how money already reads '/month', or 'a year'? Recommended: 'per'.

10. New: should a lower-case 'm2'/'m3' after a number ('a 50 m2 flat', common in European listings) be read 'square meters'/'cubic meters', with the guards in the square/cubic rule? Recommended: yes, narrowly.
review_notes: 1. Harness blocker, which affects every area: a 'says' written with a hyphenated number word can never pass. The stack reads '25' as two words ('twˈɛnti fˈIv') but 'twenty-five' as one ('twˈɛntifˌIv'), and loose() keeps spaces. In GB the vowel differs too: 'ninety-nine' gives 'nˌIntɪnˈIn' and '99' gives 'nˈInti nˈIn'. Evidence: 'It hit 45°C in Seville.' and 'Each tablet contains 25 mcg.' read correctly today, yet both fail as written and pass once the hyphen is split. core-readings' '$4.99' → 'four ninety-nine' will fail for the same reason even after the money rule ships. Recommended fix: have the phonemizer read hyphenated number words ('twenty-five', 'ninety-nine') exactly like the digits, which also fixes ordinary prose. The fallback is to split them in SpeechTest before phonemizing. I kept the hyphens in 'says', as the format requires.

2. Baseline moved while I worked. fix3/reading merged (HEAD b06b926, binary 14:59) and added Ω, kΩ, µF, µg, mcg, tbsp, Tbsp, tsp, qt, gal, doz, yr, yrs, ²/³ areas, m/s², heights and fraction-before-unit readings. Of the author's set, Ω, µF, yrs, Tbsp, qt, m², m³, µg and m/s² now pass, plus 'tbsp. of' and 'ft. long'. The author's claims that these 'fail today' are out of date, and the notes now say 'already right today'. Current totals: 17/115 (US) and 16/113 (GB) as written; 19 and 18 with number hyphens split. Every remaining failure is the missing unit rule. I checked each 'want' line by hand: all plain words read correctly in both voices (kilohms, hectopascals, millimoles, newton meters, nautical miles, kilocalories, centiliters, carat = karat, 'pee ess eye' = 'P S I').
4. Replaced 'It's a 2-min read' with 'a 5-min walk': 'read' is a heteronym ('read' as in 'red' versus 'reed'), and the two sides took different readings.

5. Tightened rules after attacking them with near-misses:
- A context: dropped current, rated, rating, battery, load, draw, motor, plug, cable and wire (each has a common non-electrical sense), and skip A before grade(s) or *. Cases: UK '12A' film rating, '5 A* grades'.
- Spaced m: a count-noun or money veto ('3 m viewers'). Glued m: dropped away, ahead and behind ('I'm 5m away' means minutes).
- L: suit sizes (42L), jeans and win-loss pairs (32W 34L, 3W 2L), US law students (1L/2L), and the 'W-2L' lookbehind.
- g: g-force ('pull 9 g') and 'rollout'. h: European clock time ('until 18h').
- Per symbol: hp in games, atm in chat, kn as kuna, MW on radio, ppm on printers, MJ as Michael Jackson, '1 mo,' as a moment, '&' after PB.
- Carat: currency veto ('$15K gold'), gold numbers limited to 9–24, kiloton veto for kt.
- Lower-case m2 slots.
Added 37 frozen near-misses for these.

6. New bugs found (the tests cover them):
- The unwrap in normalize(skippingMarkedSpans:) drops a lexicon unit's reading before '/': '300 kWh/yr' reads 'kwer', '5 mm/s' reads 'five m S', '20 ms/frame' is garbled.
- Glued '7GB/s' reads 'G B S'.
- The new heights rule eats coordinates: 40°42'46"N reads 'forty-two foot forty-six'.
- 'nm' reads 'nanometers offshore'.
- 'a 4 min mile' reads 'four minutes mile'.
- '1½ tsp' spells out tsp.
- 'Order 5 min, 10 max' reads 'five minutes', an existing false positive. Not frozen.

8. Frozen: kept 44 of the author's 47. Dropped 'See Section 3 A' (a duplicate of core-readings' 'Section 5 A'), 'The kids are 5 and 6.' (no unit-like token) and 'Posted at 5 PM.' (the times area). Total: 81. I didn't freeze candidates whose current reading is wrong: '5 Vs' reads 'versus', '50 ct' reads 'court', 'iPhone 5s' reads 'fives', '3 pt shot' is letters. Five frozen cases deliberately lock imperfect readings, and their notes say when to refreeze: A as 'uh' (×4) and 'until 18h'.

Files: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-claremccormack-Sites-readaloud--claude-worktrees-app-monetization-payments-2fe731/d937b965-6e6d-417c-ba43-5dde5061f672/scratchpad/units_review/doc.json holds both lists in --speech-test shape. In the same folder: build.py and build_frozen.py (generators), cmp2.py (the comparison, with and without hyphen splitting), and frz_us.txt / frz_gb.txt (today's frozen phonemes). The repo was not edited.
Linear: no update needed. I'm a subagent; the parent owns FIN-889.

In plain English: I checked and fixed the reading tests for measurements (metres, grams, volts, square feet, map coordinates and so on). I swapped out numbers people say two ways, added about 35 everyday examples and 37 'trap' sentences that must not change (a film rated 12A, jeans sized 32W 34L, a law student called a 1L, '5W-30' oil), and tightened the rules so they don't misfire on those. One thing to fix first: the test checker currently fails any expected answer that contains a hyphenated number like 'twenty-five', even when the app reads it perfectly. That affects every area's tests, so it needs fixing before these results mean anything. Ten small wording decisions are listed as open questions, each with a recommendation. Nothing to test in the app yet.
